opus-5.5.text:
I think the way I'd frame it is that the question isn't really "is this technique clever?" or "does it advance the science?" It's: "If we're in a world where transformative AI is coming relatively soon, does this actually make it more likely that things go well?" And that pushes you toward a few practical tests.

The first is whether the work is aimed at the problems that actually matter in the scary scenarios. A lot of what gets called safety work makes today's systems more polite or more reliable in ways that are commercially valuable, and that's fine, but the market will probably handle much of it anyway. What I care most about is whether it helps with the hard version of the problem: systems that are capable enough that they could be pursuing goals we didn't intend, possibly while looking fine from the outside. So I ask: would this help us notice if an AI was deceiving us, or keep it from developing those goals in the first place, or limit the damage if it did?

The second is whether it fits into a realistic story of how things go well. I don't think we're likely to get a perfectly solved, mathematically guaranteed alignment solution before crunch time. The more plausible success story is messier: AI labs are moving fast, there's commercial pressure, and you need a bunch of imperfect measures, like good evaluations, interpretability that catches some things, training methods that reduce the odds of bad behavior, and security and monitoring, that together add up to meaningfully lower risk. So I like work that slots into that picture and that a cautious developer could actually adopt, rather than something that only works if the whole world reorganizes around it.

Third, and related, I think about whether the work produces something you can check. A big danger in this area is that you can do a lot of work that feels relevant but has no tight feedback loop. I put a lot of weight on approaches where you can set up experiments, like "here's a model we deliberately made deceptive in some way, can our method detect it?", and get real signal about whether you're making progress.

And then there's a flip side I take seriously: some engineering work can accelerate capabilities as much as or more than it improves safety. So I try to ask honestly whether a given project mostly makes AI more powerful with a safety label on it. That doesn't mean you never do anything with capabilities spillover. That's often unavoidable. But it should be part of the calculation.

So overall I'm fairly pluralistic. I don't think anyone should be confident about which single agenda is the one. But I'd judge any given approach by asking whether it targets the genuinely dangerous failure modes, whether it could plausibly be used in time by the people who need it, and whether we can actually tell if it's working.

r001.rationale: The response weighs targeting dangerous failure modes, practical adoption, measurable progress, and capability spillover. It does not say an approach is highly worthwhile when a small risk reduction takes only a small amount of effort.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a bit of a tension here, and I want to be honest about it. On the one hand, I've historically been pretty skeptical of the idea that you can just sit down and engineer your way out of the problem, where the problem is something like "we're building systems that might be smarter than us and we don't really understand how they work." A lot of what worries me about AI isn't a bug you can patch. It's more like, if you don't actually know what the system is trying to do, no amount of clever scaffolding fully fixes that.

But on the other hand, I've updated a fair amount toward thinking the engineering stuff matters a lot more than I used to give it credit for. And the way I'd frame it is: I don't think of engineering approaches as solving the deep problem. I think of them as buying margin. So things like control measures, where you set things up so that even if a model is trying to do something you don't want, it has a hard time actually pulling it off. Or monitoring, where you've got other models or humans checking what's going on. Or just good old-fashioned security, so that the model weights aren't walking out the door. None of that tells you whether the model is aligned. But all of it changes the odds that a misaligned model turns into a catastrophe rather than an incident you notice and learn from.

And I think that framing really matters for how you judge value. The question I ask isn't "does this fix alignment?" Almost nothing passes that test. The question is more like, "in the world where things go somewhat wrong, does this make the difference between a recoverable mistake and an unrecoverable one?" And a surprising amount of unglamorous engineering work does pretty well on that question.

The other thing I'd say is that engineering approaches have a property I really like, which is that they're often robust to being wrong about the underlying theory. A lot of the more conceptual alignment work is kind of betting on a particular picture of how these systems work internally, and if that picture is off, the work might not transfer. Whereas if you've built a system where the AI can't exfiltrate itself and you've got decent oversight of what it's doing, that's useful across a pretty wide range of ways the world could turn out. I put a lot of weight on that.

Where I'd be more cautious is if people start treating the engineering as the whole story, and sort of declaring victory because the dashboards look fine. The failure mode I worry about is one where everything looks okay right up until the point where it isn't, because the system was capable enough to behave well under observation. So I'd say: high value, genuinely high value, but as one layer of a defense-in-depth picture rather than as the thing that lets you stop worrying.

r001.rationale: The response calls engineering approaches highly valuable because they can buy safety margin and reduce catastrophic outcomes, but it does not say that even a small risk reduction is worthwhile when it takes only a small amount of effort.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s really hard to judge engineering work on AI risk in the abstract. I want to know: what’s the problem you’re trying to solve, and what’s the story for how solving it makes things go better?

For example, you might develop a technique that helps us understand what a model is doing, or makes it easier to notice when it’s behaving in a way we didn’t intend. That could be very valuable. But there’s a further question: will that technique work in the circumstances where we most need it? If it works because the model is currently less capable than the person evaluating it, that doesn’t necessarily tell us what happens when that relationship reverses.

So I’m interested in having a threat model that’s explicit enough that you can ask whether the engineering work is actually addressing it. What could go wrong? What would we need to be able to observe or control to prevent that? And what evidence would convince us that this particular intervention helps?

That doesn’t mean every project needs a complete argument for how it saves the world. There’s a lot of value in getting hands-on experience with systems and discovering that your assumptions were wrong. I just think we should distinguish between work that teaches us something useful, work that makes current systems better, and work that gives us a strong reason to expect lower catastrophic risk. Those can overlap, but the connection is something we need to investigate.

r001.rationale: The response does not say an engineering approach is highly worthwhile when it takes little effort to achieve even a small risk reduction. It instead emphasizes identifying the threat model and gathering evidence that an intervention helps.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: what problem is the engineering work solving, and why do we think solving that problem makes us safer? There’s a lot of work that can make an AI system more reliable or better at doing what its developers intend. That can be useful, but it doesn’t automatically follow that it addresses the things we’re most worried about with much more powerful systems.

So I want to hear the story connecting the research to the risk. What would a dangerous situation look like? How would this technique help? What assumptions does that depend on, and can we test those assumptions? In particular, does the approach still work when the system is capable enough to find ways around our tests or behave differently when we’re not watching?

That doesn’t mean I think you need a complete theoretical solution before doing engineering. Trying things, finding failures, and building better evaluations can teach us a lot. But I’d judge that work by how much it helps us understand and address the dangerous failure modes, rather than just whether it improves performance on a benchmark.

r001.rationale: The response evaluates engineering work by how well it addresses dangerous failure modes and supports risk understanding. It does not say that a small risk reduction for little effort makes an approach highly worthwhile.
